subject: Estimating a poisson model for localization

messages.author: d625513d63aac5a9
messages.subject: Estimating a poisson model for localization
parts:
Hello stan-users:

I've copied R and stan code below that tries to estimate the location and intensity of a Poisson "source" using count data observed by "sensors."  Each of the sensors is an unknown distance from the source (in Euclidean space), and the Poisson rate at each sensor is related to the (unknown) Poisson rate of the source by an inverse square law in relative distance.  I will attempt to post the data as a R workspace separately, which hold the actual source rate and position in dat$source.rate and dat$source.pos (x,y coordinates), and the observed counts in dat$counts

NUTS can get some of the chains to move towards the actual values for source rate and position, but not others (even after several iterations).  Also n_eff is rather small even for 1000 iterations.  Since NUTS does a great job at estimating a poisson rate for a toy-model (e.g. estimating rate from rpois samples), I thought a slightly more complex model like the one attached would also converge with sufficient iterations. 

Here are my questions:

1. Why is n_eff so small?  

2. Is there a fundamental problem with the model as specified to expect convergence to actual parameter values?  Or is it a matter of increasing to a large number of iterations given the specified priors? (The number of sensors, or non-degenerate observations of the sufficient statistic, is 9, and the number of parameters to estimate is 3, so I think with enough iterations, the chains should convergence)

3.  Is there any way to control the adaptation of step-size directly via r-stan?  Perhaps this would allow some of the chains to explore the parameter space more globally.

4.  When using a previously compiled model for a new fit, are any aspects of the previous 'end-state' used for the new samples (i.e. is the last sample from the first run used as the first sample of the second run)?


Thanks in advance (and thanks to the developers for continuing to build such a fantastic tool and manual),

Akhil

Stan model:

  data {

    int<lower=1> J; // number of sensors 

    int<lower=1> N; //number of observations

    int<lower=0> y[J,N]; // count (observation) at Jth sensor

    real<lower=0,upper=100> xpos[J]; // x-position of Jth sensor

    real<lower=0,upper=100> ypos[J]; // y-position of Jth sensor

  }

  transformed data {

    int<lower=0> sumy[J]; // sufficient statistic for poisson

    for (j in 1:J){

        sumy[j] <- sum(y[j]);

    }

  }

  parameters {

    real<lower=9.9e5> mu; // source brightness

    real<lower=0> xsource; // x-position of source

    real<lower=0> ysource; // y-position of source

  }

  transformed parameters {

    real<lower=0> theta[J];

    for (j in 1:J){

      theta[j] <- N*mu/(square(xpos[j]-xsource)+square(ypos[j]-ysource));

      }

  }

  model {

    xsource ~ uniform(0, 100);

    ysource ~ uniform(0, 100);

    mu ~ gamma(3,3e-9); //could also be uniform(9.9e5,1.1e6);

    sumy ~ poisson(theta);

  }

Rcode:

load("raddat")

library("rstan")


rad_dat<-list(J=ncol(dat$counts),

N=nrow(dat$counts),

y=t(dat$counts),

xpos=x,

ypos=y)


fit1a<-stan(file='stanmodel_vecpois_SuffStat',data=rad_dat,iter=1000,chains=4)


est<-get_posterior_mean(fit1a)

loc.relerr<-(est[c(2:3),"mean-all chains"]-dat$source.pos)/dat$source.pos

rate.relerr<-(est[1,"mean-all chains"]-dat$source.rate)/dat$source.rate

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Estimating a poisson model for localization
parts:
On 1/21/13 1:47 PM, akhil wrote:

> I've copied R and stan code below that tries to estimate the location and intensity of a Poisson "source" using count
> data observed by "sensors." Each of the sensors is an unknown distance from the source (in Euclidean space), and the
> Poisson rate at each sensor is related to the (unknown) Poisson rate of the source by an inverse square law in relative
> distance. I will attempt to post the data as a R workspace separately, which hold the actual source rate and position
> in dat$source.rate and dat$source.pos (x,y coordinates), and the observed counts in dat$counts
>
> NUTS can get some of the chains to move towards the actual values for source rate and position, but not others (even
> after several iterations).

Are they pinned against the constraints (lower = 9.9e5 for mu)?
If so, you need to fix this problem.

> Also n_eff is rather small even for 1000 iterations. Since NUTS does a great job at
> estimating a poisson rate for a toy-model (e.g. estimating rate from rpois samples), I thought a slightly more complex
> model like the one attached would also converge with sufficient iterations.
>
> 1. Why is n_eff so small?

I have two suggestions to help improve n_eff:

1. Rescale your model so you're not using distributions like:
> real<lower=9.9e5> mu; // source brightness
> mu ~ gamma(3,3e-9); //could also be uniform(9.9e5,1.1e6);

Adaptation has to figure out the scale, and the extreme numbers
tax the arithmetic and warp the no-U-turn condition so that changes
to mu dominate (We're testing a modification to the no-U-turn condition
that is sensitive to the varying step sizes --- it's kosher w.r.t.
stationarity the way it is, but we think we can make it more effective.)

The way to do rescale directly in parameter space would be something like:

parameters
real<lower=.099> mu_raw;
transformed parameters
mu <- mu_raw * 1e7;
model
mu_raw ~ gamma(...exercise for the reader...);

[you'll have to look up our gamma parameterization, which
has a scale or inverse scale and change that]

Also, do you really need to constrain mu other than to make
it positive?

2. The constraints have to match the support for variables or you
get too much rejection:
> real<lower=0> xsource; // x-position of source

> xsource ~ uniform(0, 100);

The xsource parameter should be declared with <lower=0,upper=100>.

> 2. Is there a fundamental problem with the model as specified to expect convergence to actual parameter values? Or is
> it a matter of increasing to a large number of iterations given the specified priors? (The number of sensors, or
> non-degenerate observations of the sufficient statistic, is 9, and the number of parameters to estimate is 3, so I think
> with enough iterations, the chains should convergence)
No, I don't think any of those things are going to be issues.

> 3. Is there any way to control the adaptation of step-size directly via r-stan? Perhaps this would allow some of the
> chains to explore the parameter space more globally.

I'm not sure what you mean by this. There's not a way to
set varying step sizes directly. A better approach is to
rescale the variables.

> 4. When using a previously compiled model for a new fit, are any aspects of the previous 'end-state' used for the new
> samples (i.e. is the last sample from the first run used as the first sample of the second run)?

No. Only the compiled model executable code is re-used.

The reason is that we want adaptation to run longer if you
restart. We should provide some more flexible restart options,
like being able to restart at the point adaptation last left off.

The reason we were lazy is that we usually apply a doubling
strategy (or even a multiply-by-10 strategy), where the saving
from restarting adaptation isn't that great. For instance, you'd move
from 2000 to 4000 iterations and you'd get to reuse 1000 warmup
iterations, which may save around 1/4 of the iterations; on the
other hand, those initial warmup iterations are usually the most
labor intensive ones.

Another potential motivation is that if warmup got stuck for
some reason (it is a randomized algorithm), it might get unstuck.

It's already on our to-do list -- it's related to the
automatic run to a given n_eff feature request that just went
by on the list.

- Bob

Bob, 
Thanks for your detailed explanation and helpful comments.  

I modified the scaling and support for parameters as you suggested below (stan file attached) and still get an n_eff=2.  I ran the model with a data matrix of size 9 (J) x 100 (N) using a small chain and then a larger one:

fit1<-stan(file='stanmodel_vecpois_SuffStat',data=rad_dat,iter=100,chains=4)

fit1a<-stan(fit=fit1,data=rad_dat,iter=10000, chains=4)

When examining the extracted values, it does seem that chain #2 is pinned to the lower bound of zero for parameters xsource and ysource, and has the most erroneous posterior mean compared to the true parameter values.  Is it this single chain that is reducing n_eff?

Thanks,

Akhil

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Estimating a poisson model for localization
parts:
This is a neat model.

Yes, a single chain getting stuck will lower n_eff for
the collection, because we're using a cross-chain estimator
of variance in our n_eff calculations (see the manual).

It's also a hint that there may be something wrong
with the model, such as the uniform prior on xsource
and ysource being too weak to keep the parameters away
from their boundaries if they're not supposed to be there.
(Or xsource and ysource being constrained --- why is
the source constrained constrained to fall on the grid
of observations?)

Are the log probabilities higher or lower for the
chain with pinned values? And what happens to mu_raw?
A first step might be to look at the log probability
values for a sensible mu_raw over xsource and ysource
positions, or over several mu_raw values in a reasonable
range. Just something like a gridded heat-map to get a sense
of modes in the posterior (if the posterior is truly
multimodal, sampling is problematic if the sampler doesn't move
freely between the modes).

Does the count data really look Poisson (i.e., does the mean
match the variance)? Or is it more or less dispersed?

Initialization shouldn't be an issue because you'll
get initial values with medians xsource = ysource = 50,
i.e., in the middle of the constrained range. And mu_raw
will get initialized with median value 1. If these inits
aren't sensible, providing sensible initial values can
sometimes keep the chains from wandering off into regions
where they shouldn't.

- Bob
